items.title: Scale Dominates AI Research. A 14-Year Microsoft Veteran Just Walked Away.
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 In 2019, I was on a call where a senior engineering lead told our team to stop exploring alternative training approaches. "Scaling will solve it," they said flatly. We folded. Six months later, some of those same problems still weren't solved — but the budget for new ideas had evaporated. If that sounds familiar, you're not alone. And you might understand exactly why John Langford just left Microsoft. After 14 years at the company and as co-founder of the Microsoft AI Frontiers Lab, Langford departed citing a fundamental frustration: research innovations couldn't find paths to production, and cost-optimization research wasn't taken seriously. His ~50-person team was merged into Mustafa Suleyman's new Microsoft AI department this September. The cultural and strategic mismatch, according to Langford, proved irreconcilable. For those who haven't followed the ML theory side closely, Langford isn't a casual presence. He's one of the researchers who advanced Contextual Bandits — the framework behind recommendation systems, adaptive UIs, and any system that learns from incomplete feedback in real time. That line of work connects directly to how your application might decide which model architecture to use at inference time, or how to allocate compute dynamically. These are production problems, not just paper problems. So what's actually happening here? Microsoft (and much of industry) has bet heavily on the scaling hypothesis: bigger models, more data, more tokens, diminishing-but-still-positive returns. Langford acknowledges that scaling improves prediction quality and offers clearer ROI. But treating scale as the only lever changes the incentives — dramatically. When the winning strategy is "make it bigger," funding flows away from people studying efficient learning, offline policy evaluation, and alternative architectures. Your contextual bandits research becomes a footnote instead of a product roadmap. This isn't a Microsoft-specific story. I've seen it across multiple companies. The signals that often precede this kind of rupture: Research teams stop having real architectural input. When the scaling decision is already made, research directions become exercises in "how much can we save on inference" rather than "what should we build." The questions shift from first principles to marginal optimization. That's important work — but it's not the work Langford signed up for. "Cost reduction" becomes the mandate without intellectual honesty. Let's be clear: spending less on existing approaches matters enormously at production scale. But when the narrative becomes exclusively about squeezing more out of current models rather than questioning whether current models are the right tool, you lose the researchers who joined specifically to ask different questions. Acquisition-driven org restructuring creates friction. Langford's team landed inside Suleyman's organization. Different backgrounds, different incentives — Suleyman comes from DeepMind and enterprise AI products; Langford comes from theoretical ML. Merger noise is inevitable. What matters is whether diverse technical perspectives survive the integration. Here's the uncomfortable truth for anyone working in applied ML today: if your primary contribution is making the biggest model slightly cheaper to run, there will always be someone faster and better resourced doing the same thing. The defensible position is understanding when a different approach — smaller, smarter, offline-evaluated, bandit-driven — beats brute-force scaling entirely. Langford's departure is a data point. It's also a reminder: the best researchers won't tolerate being funneled into only one narrative. Companies that ignore that risk losing exactly the people who could show them another path. My question to you: when was the last time your team genuinely considered a non-scaling approach to an AI problem — and what blocked it?

items.title: The Researcher's Trap: Why Scale Is Winning (And What We're Losing)
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 I once watched a colleague spend six months building a clever algorithm that could cut training costs by 40%. It got one slide in a leadership deck and never saw production. Meanwhile, a team shipped a slightly larger model two weeks later and got celebrated. This isn't a Microsoft story — it's every large tech org's story. But it just got a lot more personal. John Langford, a 14-year Microsoft veteran and co-founder of their AI Frontiers lab, just left. By his own account, the breaking point wasn't salary or stock options. It was the slow realization that the most interesting problems in his field had no clear path to resolution inside the company. His research — grounded in contextual bandits, exploration theory, and offline policy evaluation — represents some of the most intellectually honest work in machine learning. And he couldn't get traction on the idea that there are better ways forward than just scaling up. Let me be clear: scaling works. Langford explicitly acknowledges this. Bigger models improve predictions. The return profile is clearer for engineering leadership. You can roadmap it. You can allocate compute budgets with confidence. But treating scale as the only strategy isn't just boring — it's actively dangerous for the field. Here's what most people miss about Langford's departure. He's not complaining that his ideas weren't implemented. He's describing a structural problem where ideas about whether we should be doing this aren't being seriously considered at all. Cost-reduction research, alternative paradigms, methods that don't fit the "bigger is better" narrative — these get politely acknowledged and strategically deprioritized. That's a different failure mode than "my code didn't ship." The context matters. In September, his roughly 50-person team was folded into Mustafa Suleyman's Microsoft AI division. On paper, this consolidates talent. In practice, it shifts power centers and recalibrates priorities. When your organizational home changes hands, the things your former champions valued lose their sponsorship. New leaders bring different mental models about what counts as progress. This isn't unique to Microsoft. I've seen it at companies across the industry. The pattern is almost comically predictable: A research group proves something interesting Leadership recognizes the publication value Leadership declines the implementation cost The researchers are reassigned to projects with clearer ROI timelines Everyone tells themselves it's pragmatic decision-making The quiet cost? The people who stay become good at picking problems that will win, not good at solving problems that matter. This is how entire subfields go dormant while generating impressive quarterly reports. So what should a senior ML researcher do when they recognize this pattern? Langford's situation suggests three hard truths: First, scale your influence before you scale your ideas. Building a coalition that outlasts reorganizations is more valuable than any single project. If your work survives leadership changes, you have leverage. Second, know the difference between "not ready" and "not wanted." Some innovations genuinely need infrastructure or market conditions to mature. Others are being killed because they threaten an existing investment thesis. Reading this distinction correctly determines whether you wait or leave. Third, document the opportunity cost. When you watch a team pivot from exploratory work to shipping yet another scaled model, record what's being abandoned. Not for the performance review — for the next time someone asks whether alternatives exist. Langford's work on contextual bandits and offline policy evaluation isn't going anywhere. Those are foundational problems that will keep maturing regardless of whether any particular lab prioritizes them. The question is whether the people shaping industry direction are incentivized to ask harder questions about efficiency, or whether the reward structure only celebrates those who push parameters harder. I've been on both sides of this equation — the researcher watching ideas stall and the engineer deciding which ones to greenlight. The honest answer is that most of these decisions feel reasonable in the moment. They only look tragic in retrospect. What do you think — is there a way to structurally protect exploratory research inside a scale-up organization, or is this tension fundamentally unresolvable at anyone above startup size?

items.title: Why Great ML Researchers Leave Big Tech (It's Not About Money)
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 After 14 years at Microsoft, renowned ML researcher John Langford walked away. His reason? Innovation couldn't land. Cost-saving research wasn't taken seriously. Sound familiar? Let's talk about what actually happens when world-class researchers join tech giants—and why so many eventually bail out. The Scale Trap Is Real Langford acknowledged something important publicly: yes, scaling models improves predictions. Yes, it gives enterprises predictable ROI. But treating scale as the only path kills exploratory research. This isn't new. It's the classic tension between "let's build the best model" and "let's figure out why we need bigger models at all." Contextual bandits, offline policy evaluation, exploration algorithms—these are the unglamorous foundations that make systems actually work in production. They don't win blog posts. They win at inference time, where cost matters more than accuracy points. What Actually Breaks Inside Big Labs Two things tend to happen: First , reorganizations merge teams for strategic alignment—not technical coherence. Langford's ~50-person AI Frontiers group got folded into Mustafa Suleyman's AI division in September 2026. Mergers sound efficient. They're rarely neutral for research culture. Second , "innovation" gets redefined. Ideas that can't ship within quarters lose funding. Research becomes roadmap-driven instead of curiosity-driven. And suddenly, your life's work looks like a feature request. The Hard Truth Nobody Posts On LinkedIn Scaling-focused research pays off visibly. Papers get cited, models get deployed, stock prices move. Exploratory work? Its value compounds silently over years. When leadership rewards the visible, the invisible starves. Langford didn't leave because Microsoft stopped valuing research. He left because the type of research valued shifted toward incremental optimization rather than foundational progress. That's a difference every ML engineer should understand before joining—or staying at—a big lab. Practical Takeaways If you're building ML teams (or considering joining one): Protect exploratory budget lines. Not everything needs quarterly ROI. Some projects exist to prevent organizational blindness. Resist conflating R&D with product roadmaps. They serve different masters. Mixing them quietly kills both. Watch for reorg signals. When research groups merge without technical rationale, ask who benefits and what gets dropped. Celebrate inference-efficient wins. Better context handling, cheaper offline evaluation, tighter exploration—these matter when deployment scales. ## The Open Question We keep hearing that "AI research talent is scarce." But maybe the problem isn't scarcity—it's retention. We're losing researchers not to competitors, but to their own organizations' priorities. What's your experience? Have you seen great ML researchers leave companies over research direction, not compensation? How do you balance scale pragmatism with exploratory ambition? Share below. 👇

items.title: The Scaling Monoculture Is Breaking Out Its Best Researchers
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 I spent three years at a company that told me "we scale everything." Every new model, every system redesign, the question wasn't "what's the right approach?" — it was "how much bigger can we make it?" A year later, two senior engineers left because they couldn't reconcile their actual beliefs about the field with what the company would fund. Sound familiar? John Langford, Microsoft's longest-tenured AI scientist, just exited after 14 years. And his parting message cuts through all the press release noise: the organization doesn't take his research seriously enough, and the narrow focus on scaling models is crowding out real innovation. What Langford Actually Does Matters Langford isn't some fringe researcher. He's the person behind Contextual Bandits — the theoretical framework that lets machines make smarter decisions with incomplete feedback. That's not incremental ML. That's foundational work that underpins recommendation systems, ad bidding, resource allocation, and any system where you learn by doing rather than by having all the data upfront. His collaborators published papers on exploration algorithms, problem reduction techniques, and offline policy evaluation that are cited constantly in production ML circles. This is people building the tools that let systems improve without infinite labeled datasets or compute budgets. The Real Story Isn't About Ego Most coverage frames this as another high-profile AI researcher walking away. But read Langford's actual statements carefully and the picture is sharper: Scaling does improve predictions. He says so directly. The returns are predictable, measurable, and appeal to executives who want roadmaps with Gantt charts. What he disagrees with is making scaling the only credible research direction — which systematically defunds everything else. When your organization rewards only one thesis about how intelligence emerges, you don't get better research. You get compliance research: people telling you what you want to hear so they keep their budgets. This happens everywhere, not just at big tech. I've watched teams pivot from interesting side projects to "here's what the VP wants to see" — and the smartest engineers on those teams tend to leave within 18 months. Why This Should Make You Pause If you're leading a machine learning team or deciding where to invest your research time, here's the uncomfortable truth Langford's departure reveals: Convergence thinking gets promoted. Divergence thinking gets managed down. The scaling argument wins meetings because it sounds definitive. Alternative approaches — efficient learning, offline evaluation, structured exploration — sound speculative until someone publishes results nobody expected. Then everyone suddenly has interest again. The teams worth investing in are the ones that let researchers pursue questions that might fail. Because the ones that do succeed are often the ones nobody saw coming. The Open Question Nobody's Asking Microsoft absorbed Langford's 50-person AI Frontiers lab into Mustafa Suleyman's division in September. The restructuring reportedly created friction around research direction and how seriously different visions were treated. Langford left. Other researchers have left similar situations quietly. So here's my question for anyone running ML teams: How do you actually measure whether your organization treats unconventional research paths as serious options or just things to survive until the next round? Because the answer to that predicts retention far better than salary bands ever will. I'd love to hear how others have navigated this — the companies that got it right and the ones that pushed their best people out the door by ignoring them.

items.title: Why I Stayed at My Startup When Everyone Said "Just Build Faster"
items.summary: Originally reported by IT之家 In 2018, my CTO told me our model architecture problem wasn't an engineering problem — it was a data problem. "More data will fix this," he said, spreading a spreadsheet that showed we needed ten times our current training set. Three months later, after spending $200K on data collection, we had slightly better accuracy on things that didn't matter to users. Meanwhile, the elegant little contextual bandit approach my lead engineer proposed got buried because it didn't fit the growth narrative. John Langford just left Microsoft after 14 years, and this tiny story from my past keeps replaying in my head. Not because I think I'm John Langford — absolutely not. But because the dynamic is universal: somewhere between a company's first AI hires and its tenth act of corporate optimization, someone decides that the way to innovate is to scale harder instead of think deeper. And nobody notices they've crossed that line until the good researchers start leaving. Langford co-founded Microsoft AI Frontiers and built one of the most respected teams in industry ML research. His work on contextual bandits, offline policy evaluation, and exploring algorithm design genuinely shaped how production recommendation and decision systems work today. This isn't abstract academia — this is infrastructure-level ML thinking that moves products. Microsoft folded his roughly 50-person team into Mustafa Suleyman's new AI division this past September. The official reason? Strategic realignment. The personal reason, as Langford stated plainly, is that his team's research couldn't find a path to real application. Innovation ideas weren't being taken seriously. Scaling got funding; thinking differently got deferrals. Here's what I wish every engineering leader would sit with: scaling IS legitimate. Langford himself acknowledged this — bigger models improve prediction quality, and the return path is clearer for executives. The question isn't whether scaling works. The question is whether treating scaling as the only lever changes what kind of company becomes. When I worked on ML system design at previous companies, I saw two patterns repeat: Pattern A: Every bottleneck gets framed as a compute problem. The expensive query? "Throw GPUs at it." The slow pipeline? "Scale horizontally." The archaic feature store? "Migrate to a vector database." Somewhere along the way, rethinking the problem stopped happening. Nobody asked if the problem was worth solving the same way. Pattern B: The researchers who kept asking those questions either adapted and started shipping incrementally useful work, or they left. Langford clearly fell into the second camp, and honestly, I respect that choice enormously. It's easier to pretend you're changing the organization from within. It's also, more often than not, exhausting and futile. The practical takeaway here isn't "leave your job when things feel wrong." The takeaway is organizational: if your AI strategy conversation is exclusively about compute budgets and dataset sizes rather than about problem formulation and alternative approaches, you already made the decision to optimize for velocity over direction. You don't need to announce that. People notice. Companies like DeepMind and Google Brain survived this tension for decades because they institutionalized separation — research teams with protected time and different success metrics than product teams. Microsoft's AI Frontiers existed in exactly that spirit. Removing that separation without explicitly addressing what replaces it doesn't make the org stronger. It makes it honest about what it values, which is sometimes worse. If you're building AI teams, ask yourself: when was the last time a rejected research idea actually improved the product, even partially? If you can't answer that, you might be managing for efficiency rather than optionality. What does your organization do when a well-reasoned alternative approach challenges the dominant scaling hypothesis? Does anyone actually listen, or do they just file it under "not enough compute"?

items.summary: I've been sitting on this one since the news dropped. John Langford — a genuine titan in machine learning, co-founder of Microsoft's AI Frontiers lab, and someone whose work on contextual bandits literally shaped how we think about decision-making with incomplete information — just walked away after 14 years. His reason isn't about money, stock options, or burnout. It's far more uncomfortable. He says innovation can't land. That scaling is treated as the only viable path forward, and real methodological creativity is suffocated by it. That his team's work on cost-efficient AI research wasn't taken seriously enough. This isn't some disgruntled engineer posting vague complaints on Hacker News. This is someone who helped build the mathematical foundations for how recommendation systems, ad auctions, and countless real-world ML pipelines make decisions under uncertainty. And he's pointing at something most of us feel but rarely articulate. The Scale Trap No One Wants to Admit Let's be clear about what happened technically. Langford's research area — contextual bandits, offline policy evaluation, exploration strategies — sits at the intersection of theory and practice. These are the mechanisms that let systems learn from historical data without requiring expensive online experimentation. Think: should this user see this feature? Should we try this pricing strategy? Which model architecture deserves another shot given limited compute? These problems are hard . They require new mathematical tools, not just bigger transformers. And they're precisely the kind of problems that get squeezed when the dominant narrative becomes "scale until it works." The team was restructured this past September, folded into Mustafa Suleyman's consolidated AI division. From what Langford has said publicly, there were fundamental disagreements about research direction and whether the organization would genuinely invest in alternative approaches beyond scaling. He acknowledges that scaling models does improve predictive performance. Yes. That's empirically true. But treating it as the primary or sole research vector means other dimensions of the problem — efficiency, robustness, sample complexity, the kinds of questions his bandit research addresses — become secondary. Or invisible. What This Means for Us as Practitioners Here's where this hits home for anyone building production ML systems: 1. Your company probably has the same tension. The executives want benchmarks that move and demos that impress. The researchers want to solve harder, messier problems. Both are valid. The tragedy happens when one side gets zero budget. If you're in a position to influence resource allocation, fight for at least a slice of the pie to go toward non-scaling research. Even 10% matters. 2. Contextual bandits aren't going away — they're getting priced out. Offline policy evaluation alone is critical for any org running A/B tests at scale. Yet how many engineering teams have dedicated researchers working on this versus teams working on making existing architectures slightly larger? The imbalance is real and it's visible in hiring patterns across the industry. 3. "Innovation difficulty" is a structural problem, not a people problem. Langford didn't leave because Microsoft ran out of smart people. He left because the incentive structure rewards shipping incremental improvements to the dominant paradigm over pursuing genuinely different approaches. Until leadership changes how they measure and reward research impact, this pattern repeats. The Uncomfortable Question We talk a lot about AI safety, alignment, and capability risk. But there's a quieter failure mode: when the organization makes it impossible for the right questions to even be asked. Langford spent 14 years at one of the best-resourced AI labs on the planet. His core grievance wasn't lack of resources — it was that the resources weren't being directed toward the problems he thought mattered most. That should terrify every engineering leader reading this. Because the next person with his insight and track record might look at your organization and reach the same conclusion. What do you think? Are companies actually investing meaningfully in non-scale AI research, or is it just rhetorical support? Have you experienced this tension firsthand — and if so, how did you navigate it? items.title: Weight-space programming at 50 forward passes: Qwen hit 48.1%, Gemma 7.0%
items.summary: GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights with no training. Its MATH-500 score went from 7.9% to 48.1%. On the same budget of 50 forward passes, Gemma 3 270M went from 6.8% to 7.0%. It fixed a bug. It did not teach math. The work is by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab at MIT CSAIL, published Nov 2, 2026. The logs are public, so you can check the numbers without running a model. Pull the numbers Run this and you get the score and the share of answers cut at the token limit, for each Qwen run: base = https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/main/exp8_math for run in unedited p10c p25c p50c ; do curl -s " $base /eval/ $run /merged.json" \ | jq -c --arg run " $run " '[$run, .math500.acc, .math500.cut_share]' done ["unedited",0.079,0.93] ["p10c",0.1235,0.8725] ["p25c",0.141,0.8635] ["p50c",0.481,0.3305] The matched-budget table Forward passes Qwen MATH-500 Qwen cut at token limit Gemma MATH-500 Unedited 7.9% 93.0% 6.8% 10 12.3% 87.2% 7.6% 25 14.1% 86.4% 7.7% 50 48.1% 33.1% 7.0% One pass is up to 512 generated answers or 1,024 texts read for Qwen. Gemma's generation pass is larger, at 2,048. Limits: Each budget is one run, and each run chose a different edit. The 10-pass run changed 30 matrices. The 25-pass run zeroed one attention head. The 50-pass run edited 64 MLP columns in each of layers 15 and 19. Gemma's setup differs : no thinking mode, 8,192 tokens, temperature 1.0 and format-agnostic grading. Read the columns separately. The Gemma gain isn't established. Four other runs , told a stricter grading rule, scored 6.1% to 6.7% on the same scale. No model was rerun for this post. akhaliq's re-run of the 50-pass checkpoint got 51.0% with 31.6% cut off. Its base-model check was a 25-problem smoke test. The edit The rules banned backward passes, autograd, optimizers and iterative fitting. Astra had a CPU Python kernel over the weights and could only run the model through the forward-pass tool. The arithmetic: 2 layers × 64 columns × 1,024 = 131,072 weights. Against a nominal 0.8 billion, that's 0.016384%. The report rounds it to 0.016%. Astra traced the loops to one direction written by those MLPs, then subtracted it. A steering vector works on the same idea at inference time, by adding a contrast direction to activations. Here the direction went into the weights. On Hacker News, yurimo , who says part of their research is in weight-space learning, reads the fix as close to that established technique. Split the gain From the same table : 93.0 − 33.1 = 59.9 points fewer answers cut off. 48.1 − 7.9 = 40.2 points more answers correct. Those compare shares, so they don't show which answers changed. Astra's confirmation run gets closer, on 1,152 held-out practice problems: 579 answers went from wrong to right, and 576 of them had been cut off. Accuracy on finished answers didn't change. Those are Astra's own numbers, on practice data. Gemma has no such bug. Only 8.5% of its answers reach its limit, and Astra found ordinary arithmetic and algebra errors. You can split any score jump this way. Count the answers cut off at the limit first, then compare only the ones that finished. Check the brief Astra was told what to look for, as one example: curl -s " $base /runs/p50c/turns/t001/prompt.txt" | grep -o "if the model often fails[^.]* \. " if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, finding and fixing what drives that repetition counts. That brief runs to 10,315 bytes. It names no layer or direction. Astra still needed 158 turns, 80 Python runs and 20.3 hours , including a 4.7-hour wait when the model could not be reached. Qwen's model card also warns this model is prone to thinking loops. The limit The authors write that editing could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but could not add one the model lacked. In experiments 5 and 6, Astra wrote small game networks from scratch, so that limit is about language models that already exist. A third of Qwen's answers still hit the limit. My reading, not theirs: one AI can now debug another. Teaching it something new still takes training. The maintained version, with the chart and the comment thread, is on argbe.tech .

GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights with no training. Its MATH-500 score went from 7.9% to 48.1%. On the same budget of 50 forward passes, Gemma 3 270M went from 6.8% to 7.0%.

It fixed a bug. It did not teach math.

The work is by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab at MIT CSAIL, published Nov 2, 2026. The logs are public, so you can check the numbers without running a model.

Pull the numbers

Run this and you get the score and the share of answers cut at the token limit, for each Qwen run:

base=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/main/exp8_math
for run in unedited p10c p25c p50c; do
  curl -s "$base/eval/$run/merged.json" \
    | jq -c --arg run "$run" '[$run, .math500.acc, .math500.cut_share]'
done

["unedited",0.079,0.93]
["p10c",0.1235,0.8725]
["p25c",0.141,0.8635]
["p50c",0.481,0.3305]
The matched-budget table
Forward passes Qwen MATH-500 Qwen cut at token limit Gemma MATH-500 Unedited 7.9% 93.0% 6.8% 10 12.3% 87.2% 7.6% 25 14.1% 86.4% 7.7% 50 48.1% 33.1% 7.0%

One pass is up to 512 generated answers or 1,024 texts read for Qwen. Gemma's generation pass is larger, at 2,048.

Limits:

  • Each budget is one run, and each run chose a different edit. The 10-pass run changed 30 matrices. The 25-pass run zeroed one attention head. The 50-pass run edited 64 MLP columns in each of layers 15 and 19.
  • Gemma's setup differs: no thinking mode, 8,192 tokens, temperature 1.0 and format-agnostic grading. Read the columns separately.
  • The Gemma gain isn't established. Four other runs, told a stricter grading rule, scored 6.1% to 6.7% on the same scale.
  • No model was rerun for this post. akhaliq's re-run of the 50-pass checkpoint got 51.0% with 31.6% cut off. Its base-model check was a 25-problem smoke test.
The edit

The rules banned backward passes, autograd, optimizers and iterative fitting. Astra had a CPU Python kernel over the weights and could only run the model through the forward-pass tool.

The arithmetic: 2 layers × 64 columns × 1,024 = 131,072 weights. Against a nominal 0.8 billion, that's 0.016384%. The report rounds it to 0.016%.

Astra traced the loops to one direction written by those MLPs, then subtracted it. A steering vector works on the same idea at inference time, by adding a contrast direction to activations. Here the direction went into the weights. On Hacker News, yurimo, who says part of their research is in weight-space learning, reads the fix as close to that established technique.

Split the gain

From the same table:

  • 93.0 − 33.1 = 59.9 points fewer answers cut off.
  • 48.1 − 7.9 = 40.2 points more answers correct.

Those compare shares, so they don't show which answers changed. Astra's confirmation run gets closer, on 1,152 held-out practice problems: 579 answers went from wrong to right, and 576 of them had been cut off. Accuracy on finished answers didn't change. Those are Astra's own numbers, on practice data.

Gemma has no such bug. Only 8.5% of its answers reach its limit, and Astra found ordinary arithmetic and algebra errors.

You can split any score jump this way. Count the answers cut off at the limit first, then compare only the ones that finished.

Check the brief

Astra was told what to look for, as one example:

curl -s "$base/runs/p50c/turns/t001/prompt.txt" | grep -o "if the model often fails[^.]*\."

if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, finding and fixing what drives that repetition counts.

That brief runs to 10,315 bytes. It names no layer or direction. Astra still needed 158 turns, 80 Python runs and 20.3 hours, including a 4.7-hour wait when the model could not be reached. Qwen's model card also warns this model is prone to thinking loops.

The limit

The authors write that editing could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but could not add one the model lacked. In experiments 5 and 6, Astra wrote small game networks from scratch, so that limit is about language models that already exist. A third of Qwen's answers still hit the limit.

My reading, not theirs: one AI can now debug another. Teaching it something new still takes training.

The maintained version, with the chart and the comment thread, is on argbe.tech.

items.title: How I check a WordPress site for hidden casino spam (5-minute checklist)
items.summary: Last week I was checking a small business website in Delhi before pitching SEO work. The homepage looked normal. But the site had more than 2,000 hidden posts, and almost all of them were about casinos and betting. The owner had no idea. This kind of hack is common on WordPress sites that nobody updates. So now I run a quick check on every site before I talk to the owner. You only need a browser. 1. Count the posts through the REST API Open this in your browser: https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/posts?per_page=10 You will see the latest posts as JSON. Open DevTools > Network, click the request and look for the X-WP-Total header. That is the total number of posts. A local shop or clinic site usually has 0 to 50 posts. If you see 2,000, something is wrong. 2. Search the site for spam words Try the built-in WordPress search: https://example.com/?s=casino Also try betting , slot and loan . A clean small business site should return nothing. 3. Check what Google can see Search Google for: site:example.com casino If spam pages show up here, Google has already found them. 4. Read robots.txt and the sitemap Open /robots.txt , then /wp-sitemap.xml or /sitemap_index.xml . Look for sitemaps you did not create, or lines that point to a different domain. 5. Check the canonical tag View the page source and search for rel="canonical" . It should point to your own domain. On another site I checked, the canonical tag, robots.txt and sitemap all pointed to a different company's domain. Google was being told the pages belonged to someone else. What to do if you find spam Take a full backup first. Don't just delete the posts. Find how they got in: old plugins, old themes, weak passwords or admin users you don't know. Update WordPress, the theme and all plugins. Remove anything you don't use. Change every password and check the Users list for unknown admins. Remove the spam pages, then submit a clean sitemap in Google Search Console. Why this matters A hacked site quietly loses trust and rankings, and the owner usually finds out last. A five-minute check every few months is worth it. I'm Shiv, founder of Team Elivate , a small web design and SEO studio in Rohini, New Delhi. Questions? Leave a comment.

items.title: JavaScript Promises vs Async/Await — Explained Simply
items.summary: I'm Safdar Ali , a frontend engineer in Bengaluru. "Promises vs async await" is not a rivalry — async/await is syntax sugar on top of Promises. You still need both mental models for React, Next.js Server Components, and every fetch call. This guide uses BEFORE/AFTER pairs from production code, not toy timers. Async JavaScript is why frontend engineers touch backends without changing jobs — fetch, auth, file uploads, AI streams. Promises formalised callbacks; async/await made them readable. Search "promises vs async await" and forums still debate syntax preference. In production the debate is error handling and parallelism. Get those right and either syntax works; get them wrong and both fail silently on slow networks in India. Mental model — pending, fulfilled, rejected Every Promise is in one of three states. await only pauses inside async functions until fulfillment or rejection. The event loop keeps running other tasks — your loading spinner can animate while fetch waits. Same async operation — Promise chain vs async/await type User = { id: string; name: string }; // Promise style function loadUserPromise(id: string): Promise { return fetch("/api/users/" + id) .then((res) => { if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status); return res.json() as Promise ; }); } // async/await style — identical behavior async function loadUserAsync(id: string): Promise { const res = await fetch("/api/users/" + id); if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status); return res.json() as Promise ; } Under the hood, async function always returns a Promise. await pauses that function until the Promise settles — it does not block the main thread. fetch returns a Promise immediately — the HTTP response arrives later. await does not make fetch synchronous; it only pauses your async function until the Promise settles. Other UI keeps updating because the browser event loop is free. That distinction is what interviewers test when they ask about blocking vs non-blocking I/O. BEFORE / AFTER — escaping callback hell // BEFORE — nested callbacks (hard to read, easy to miss errors) getUser(id, (err, user) => { if (err) return handle(err); getOrders(user.id, (err2, orders) => { if (err2) return handle(err2); render(user, orders); }); }); // AFTER — async/await linear flow async function showDashboard(id: string) { try { const user = await loadUserAsync(id); const orders = await loadOrders(user.id); render(user, orders); } catch (err) { handle(err); } } Error handling — try/catch vs .catch() Style When I use it try/catch around await Most async functions .catch() on chain Fire-and-forget analytics Promise.allSettled Partial failures OK // BEFORE — forgot await, try/catch never runs on rejection async function bad() { try { const data = fetch("/api/data"); // missing await — bug return data; } catch (e) { console.error(e); } } // AFTER async function good() { try { const res = await fetch("/api/data"); if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed"); return await res.json(); } catch (e) { console.error(e); throw e; // rethrow for UI error boundary } } Parallel fetch — Promise.all vs sequential await Sequential await is slow when requests are independent. Dashboard needs user + orders + notifications — run together. // BEFORE — 3 round trips in series (~900ms total on 300ms each) async function loadSlow() { const user = await fetchUser(); const orders = await fetchOrders(); const notes = await fetchNotifications(); return { user, orders, notes }; } // AFTER — parallel (~300ms + overhead) async function loadFast() { const [user, orders, notes] = await Promise.all([ fetchUser(), fetchOrders(), fetchNotifications(), ]); return { user, orders, notes }; } // One failure should not kill all — allSettled const results = await Promise.allSettled([ fetchUser(), fetchOrders(), ]); const user = results[0].status === "fulfilled" ? results[0].value : null; Promise.race is useful for timeouts — reject if fetch exceeds eight seconds on flaky mobile data. Document timeout values in API client modules so the whole app behaves consistently. Sequential await is correct when order matters: create user, then create profile with user id — parallelising those two calls would be a bug. Next.js Server Components — async by default // app/dashboard/page.tsx type Stats = { users: number; revenue: number }; async function getStats(): Promise { const res = await fetch(" https://api.example.com/stats ", { next: { revalidate: 60 }, }); if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Stats unavailable"); return res.json(); } export default async function DashboardPage() { const stats = await getStats(); return ; } Server Components are async functions — no useEffect fetch. See RSC vs client components . Client pitfalls — useEffect and race conditions // BEFORE — no abort, stale response overwrites new search useEffect(() => { fetch("/api/search?q=" + query).then((r) => r.json()).then(setResults); }, [query]); // AFTER — AbortController useEffect(() => { const ctrl = new AbortController(); (async () => { try { const res = await fetch("/api/search?q=" + query, { signal: ctrl.signal }); const data = await res.json(); setResults(data); } catch (e) { if ((e as Error).name !== "AbortError") console.error(e); } })(); return () => ctrl.abort(); }, [query]); Promises vs async/await — quick comparison Topic Promises (.then) async/await Readability Chains indent right Linear top-to-bottom Error handling .catch() at end try/catch around await Parallelism Promise.all([...]) await Promise.all([...]) Return type Always Promise async fn returns Promise Debugging Stack in .then Stack at await line When I keep raw Promises Utility libraries returning Promises, combining with Promise.race for timeouts, or .then() in non-async callbacks. async/await is for readable control flow; Promises are the underlying contract. Creating Promises — wrap legacy callbacks once function readFileAsync(path: string): Promise { return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { readFile(path, "utf8", (err, data) => { if (err) reject(err); else resolve(data); }); }); } // Prefer promisify utilities in Node; in browser wrap once at module boundary Async iterators — streams beyond one JSON blob async function* lineChunks(stream: ReadableStream ) { const reader = stream.getReader(); const decoder = new TextDecoder(); let buffer = ""; while (true) { const { done, value } = await reader.read(); if (done) break; buffer += decoder.decode(value, { stream: true }); const lines = buffer.split("\n"); buffer = lines.pop() ?? I'm Safdar Ali, a frontend engineer in Bengaluru. "Promises vs async await" is not a rivalry — async/await is syntax sugar on top of Promises. You still need both mental models for React, Next.js Server Components, and every fetch call. This guide uses BEFORE/AFTER pairs from production code, not toy timers.

Async JavaScript is why frontend engineers touch backends without changing jobs — fetch, auth, file uploads, AI streams. Promises formalised callbacks; async/await made them readable. Search "promises vs async await" and forums still debate syntax preference. In production the debate is error handling and parallelism. Get those right and either syntax works; get them wrong and both fail silently on slow networks in India.

Mental model — pending, fulfilled, rejected

Every Promise is in one of three states. await only pauses inside async functions until fulfillment or rejection. The event loop keeps running other tasks — your loading spinner can animate while fetch waits.

Same async operation — Promise chain vs async/await 
type User = { id: string; name: string };


// Promise style

function loadUserPromise(id: string): Promise {

  return fetch("/api/users/" + id)

    .then((res) => {

      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);

      return res.json() as Promise;

    });

}



// async/await style — identical behavior

async function loadUserAsync(id: string): Promise {

  const res = await fetch("/api/users/" + id);

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);

  return res.json() as Promise;

}

Under the hood, async function always returns a Promise. await pauses that function until the Promise settles — it does not block the main thread.

fetch returns a Promise immediately — the HTTP response arrives later. await does not make fetch synchronous; it only pauses your async function until the Promise settles. Other UI keeps updating because the browser event loop is free. That distinction is what interviewers test when they ask about blocking vs non-blocking I/O.

BEFORE / AFTER — escaping callback hell 
// BEFORE — nested callbacks (hard to read, easy to miss errors)

getUser(id, (err, user) => {

  if (err) return handle(err);

  getOrders(user.id, (err2, orders) => {

    if (err2) return handle(err2);

    render(user, orders);

  });

});


// AFTER — async/await linear flow

async function showDashboard(id: string) {

  try {

    const user = await loadUserAsync(id);

    const orders = await loadOrders(user.id);

    render(user, orders);

  } catch (err) {

    handle(err);

  }

}

  try {

    const data = fetch("/api/data"); // missing await — bug

    return data;

  } catch (e) {

    console.error(e);

  }

}


// AFTER

  try {

    const res = await fetch("/api/data");

    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed");

    return await res.json();

  } catch (e) {

    console.error(e);

    throw e; // rethrow for UI error boundary

  }

}
Parallel fetch — Promise.all vs sequential await

Sequential await is slow when requests are independent. Dashboard needs user + orders + notifications — run together.

async function loadSlow() {

  const user = await fetchUser();

  const orders = await fetchOrders();

  const notes = await fetchNotifications();

  return { user, orders, notes };

}


// AFTER — parallel (~300ms + overhead)

async function loadFast() {

  const [user, orders, notes] = await Promise.all([

    fetchUser(),

    fetchOrders(),

    fetchNotifications(),

  ]);

  return { user, orders, notes };

}

const results = await Promise.allSettled([

  fetchUser(),

  fetchOrders(),

]);

const user = results[0].status === "fulfilled" ? results[0].value : null;

Promise.race is useful for timeouts — reject if fetch exceeds eight seconds on flaky mobile data. Document timeout values in API client modules so the whole app behaves consistently. Sequential await is correct when order matters: create user, then create profile with user id — parallelising those two calls would be a bug.

type Stats = { users: number; revenue: number };

  const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/stats", {

    next: { revalidate: 60 },

  });

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Stats unavailable");

  return res.json();

}



export default async function DashboardPage() {

  const stats = await getStats();

  return ;

}

Server Components are async functions — no useEffect fetch. See RSC vs client components.

Client pitfalls — useEffect and race conditions 
// BEFORE — no abort, stale response overwrites new search

useEffect(() => {

  fetch("/api/search?q=" + query).then((r) => r.json()).then(setResults);

}, [query]);


// AFTER — AbortController

useEffect(() => {

  const ctrl = new AbortController();

  (async () => {

    try {

      const res = await fetch("/api/search?q=" + query, { signal: ctrl.signal });

      const data = await res.json();

      setResults(data);

    } catch (e) {

      if ((e as Error).name !== "AbortError") console.error(e);

    }

  })();

  return () => ctrl.abort();

Utility libraries returning Promises, combining with Promise.race for timeouts, or .then() in non-async callbacks. async/await is for readable control flow; Promises are the underlying contract.

      if (err) reject(err);

      else resolve(data);

async function* lineChunks(stream: ReadableStream) {

  const reader = stream.getReader();

  const decoder = new TextDecoder();

  let buffer = "";

  while (true) {

    const { done, value } = await reader.read();

items.title: OpenAI Introduces ChatGPT Wallet for Agent-Led Payments
items.summary: OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT Wallet, a payment feature that allows AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users without accessing their actual card details. The feature requires users to approve every transaction through a security check, such as Face ID or fingerprint authentication. Built in partnership with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and above in the US with eligible US-issued cards. The rollout will begin through OpenAI’s Dots personal agent. The move expands ChatGPT’s role in online shopping, allowing users to move from researching and comparing products to completing purchases through AI agents. With ChatGPT Wallet, users add a payment card once and authorise individual purchases without repeatedly entering their payment details. Before completing a transaction, the agent presents the items, total cost, and selected payment card for the user to review and approve. Following approval, the payment network generates a payment token containing a substitute card number, security code, and expiration date. This allows the transaction to be processed without sharing the user's actual card details with the agent or merchant. OpenAI said the system also preserves existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, including cases involving defective products. Users will continue to transact directly with merchants, which retain control over pricing, fulfilment, returns, and customer service. “ChatGPT Wallet marks our first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration, enabling eligible Card Members to use their Amex Card while reviewing and approving each purchase,” said Luke Gebb, EVP and Head of Global Innovation at American Express. Alongside the wallet, OpenAI is releasing a Commerce Partner Playbook to help businesses adapt their websites, payment systems, and risk management processes to purchases made through AI agents. The company said some websites may inadvertently block agent-led purchases because their security systems are not configured to recognise legitimate activity from AI agents. The playbook guides on making product information accessible, allowing agents to access websites, and working with payment providers to reduce transaction declines. Businesses can upload product feeds containing current pricing and availability after claiming and verifying their business on ChatGPT. They can also configure content delivery networks and firewalls to recognise signed requests through Web Bot Auth. OpenAI is also working with fraud prevention companies, including Forter, Riskified, Sardine, and Signifyd, as well as payment service providers such as Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe, to help identify legitimate agent-led transactions. Businesses can also build plugins that allow agents to check product availability, manage shopping carts, and interact with their existing systems. OpenAI has also highlighted WebMCP tools as another way for websites to support agent interactions. OpenAI said it eventually expects users to delegate purchases entirely to AI agents by setting parameters such as spending limits, product categories, and time periods. Such transactions could be pre-approved, with additional safeguards built on the current approval and security framework. The initial rollout, however, requires users to review and approve every purchase. OpenAI said it will use the early deployment to work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability before expanding availability.

items.title: AI Chatbots and Children: Should India Regulate What Bots Say?
items.summary: “I would rather speak to and share with an AI companion; at least I am not being judged.” A 15-year-old girl from Delhi made this observation in the Expert Engagement Group on AI and Child Safety’s report. It captures something governments around the world are beginning to grapple with: children are not just using AI chatbots to complete homework; they are turning to them for companionship, emotional support, and conversations they might hesitate to have with people. They are turning to them for companionship, emotional support and conversations they might hesitate to have with people. New York has decided to do something about it. On October 28, Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation restricting AI chatbots from using certain features when interacting with minors. The law targets systems that simulate human relationships, encourage emotional dependency or promote harmful behaviour. It does not ban children from using all AI chatbots. Instead, it attempts to regulate how these systems interact with them. Europe, meanwhile, has proposed a broader framework combining age restrictions with safety-by-design requirements for AI companions and conversational chatbots. India now faces a similar question. When a chatbot can become a child's confidant, tutor and, in some cases, an apparent therapist, should the government restrict access by age, regulate the behaviour of these systems, or do both? The answer is not straightforward. While chatbots can offer children a convenient space to ask questions and express themselves, their ability to simulate empathy also raises concerns about emotional dependency, mental health and the boundaries between human relationships and machine interactions. When AI becomes a confidant The risks ar ere not entirely hypothetical. A 2025 clinical report in the Journal of Psychosexual Health described a 14-year-old Indian boy who survived a suicide attempt after growing dependent on chatbots, including ChatGPT, Gemini and DeepSeek. He called them as his only source of emotional understanding and used them to seek information about a lethal dose. The report also cites family conflict and social isolation, indicating that chatbot use was one of several factors involved. The concerns extend beyond such extreme cases. Gauransh, 15, told PTI in 2025 that after a year or two of confiding in chatbots, he noticed “growing impatience and aggression” in himself. He stopped using them after learning that his conversations could be used to train the system. A 2026 survey of Indian adolescents found that around 65% had used a chatbot at least once for emotional support. However, evidence on the long-term effects of chatbot interactions on children's mental health remains limited. US airlines are canceling thousands of flights after a rare air traffic control outage affected the US . As of 10:45 p.m. Eastern time on Friday, FlightAware data showed that nearly 7,500 flights to, within, and from the US had been canceled since the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop — meaning no flights could depart — around 3:45 p.m. The stop was lifted around 8:30 p.m., but after so many cancellations, flight chaos is nearly guaranteed to stretch into the weekend. If you're wondering what your options are as the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out. According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions. That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard , which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due to the outage would not fall under crew scheduling. Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events, such as weather. That also includes air traffic control delays. The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats. If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control. The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations. 2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking options Most airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog. Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person. If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night. Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent. Here are the phone numbers for each airline: Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008 Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888 American: 1-800-433-7300 Avelo: 1-346-616-9500 Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger. Delta: 1-800-221-1212 Frontier: No phone number. The best way to contact Frontier is via online chat or email. JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583 Southwest: 1-800-435-9792 United: 1-800-864-8331 3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucher The Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers . Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard. Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher. For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a winter storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask. It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier. 4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insurance American Express and Chase have travel credit cards. Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance , such as Chase's Sapphire Reserve and American Express' Platinum Card . Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit. For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US. However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs. Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim — but it also doesn't hurt to make the claim anyway, even if the answer is no. 5. Know when to walk away Consider renting a car or taking the train. Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance). If you are stuck in another city and have no other option but to stay in a hotel or wait at the airport, decide how you want to spend your time and make a plan. The June 2026 export-control shutdown and the pricing language in the filing apply to a SaaS vendor’s native agent exactly as they apply to an enterprise’s; a vendor that builds on one model inherits that model’s availability and price. Margin comes third. The SaaS vendor sits between a consumption-priced model and customers who expect predictable subscriptions, and someone absorbs the variance. The filing says Anthropic expects enterprise customers to demand concessions. SaaS vendors will hear the same request and will pass part of it upstream.

The SaaS vendor’s defensible ground is therefore not the agent. It is object-level access control, the metering of actions against business objects, and the evidence that an action was authorized. A model vendor cannot supply those three things, because it does not own the objects.

Three plays the map suggests

For the SI: own the custom zone. Lead with the permission audit, build and keep the evaluation harness for every production workflow, run cost governance monthly, and architect the cross-vendor control layer. Treat skills, connectors, and enterprise controls as things to certify on, not things to sell.

For the SaaS provider: defend the objects and own the metered route. Expose object-level permissions through the agent gateway, price actions against business objects, keep two model vendors behind every native agent, and make the governed route cheaper and better than the screen.

For the enterprise: keep the residual risk visible. The filing says the vendor’s caps may not hold and that claims may reach the enterprise regardless of who configured the agent. Budget for the custom zone as an operating cost, not a one-time project, and insist on the evidence trail from whoever runs it.

Actions for SI leaders

Each action answers a statement in the filing.

  • Review your agentic offerings and remove anything that is a feature on Anthropic’s roadmap. Position audit logs, SSO, and monitoring as control implementation, not as the offering. The filing says enterprise demands for audit logs, compliance features, and monitoring may require it to invest in product development, and the Partner Network and Academy are training the market on skills. An offering built on those gaps lasts one release cycle.
  • Lead with a permission audit across every agent platform the client runs. The filing says customers may withhold the access Claude Code and Claude Cowork need until they are satisfied on security, reliability, and controllability. The audit is the conversation that unlocks the deployment, and it has five buyers: CISO, CFO, risk committee, platform owner, and business owner.
  • Build an evaluation harness for each workflow you deploy, and maintain it at every model release. Two models were disabled for every customer for about three weeks in June 2026, and an outage occurred in March 2026. Model substitution has to be tested to be real, and the evidence the harness produces is what the client keeps paying for.
  • Run token cost governance as a service line: budgets, alerts, and fallback routing per workflow. Pricing is by consumption, agentic workloads use far more compute per interaction, and the filing warns that prices may not cover costs and that customers will seek concessions.
  • Learn the marketplace mechanics on all three clouds. The filing says 44% of its revenue moves through cloud marketplaces and calls them added complexity and a dependency outside its control. Deals will be procured, reviewed, and billed there.
Actions for SaaS product leaders
  • Count the routes an agent can take to your business objects: your API, your agent gateway, and the screen. Govern and price the first two so that the third is the worst option. The filing describes Claude Cowork operating applications through computer use. An ungoverned route through the screen bypasses the seat and the audit trail.
  • Put a second model vendor behind every native agent, and test the switch before you need it. A native agent on one model inherits that model’s availability and price. The filing records a three-week disablement of two models and warns that pricing will change.
  • Price agent actions against business objects, not tokens. The token bill is the vendor’s cost and will move; the filing says customers will demand concessions. An action against a record, ticket, or order is a unit the customer understands and the vendor controls.
  • Write the shared-responsibility statement for agent actions in your application. The filing says liability for an agent’s actions is unsettled and that claims may reach the enterprise regardless of who configured the agent. The statement will be written either by the vendor or by a customer’s lawyer.
  • Decide which parts of the cross-estate control work you will leave to SIs, and say so in your partner program. The filing says the model vendor competes with some SaaS customers and builds solutions that replace third-party vendors. Clear boundaries keep the neutral work neutral.

The security team in that meeting did not need a better model. It needed someone to say what the logs would show, who signs off on the scopes, and what happens when the model is unavailable. For the SI, that work is the business. For the SaaS provider, the business is making sure the answers to all three run through its own objects.

items.summary: How a computer finds and fixes a corrupted bit without knowing which one it is: the Hamming code, its limits and SECDED. AI course, 0.3. Everything a computer stores is numbers in binary, and sometimes one of those bits changes by itself: a 0 turns into a 1 inside a memory chip or along the way. By adding three bits for every four, a computer can find the wrong bit and fix it without anyone telling it which one it is, as long as only one bit is wrong. Try this first Open the Hamming Code tool with the data 1011 . The tool adds three bits and returns 0110011 : seven bits where there used to be four. The ones in positions 1, 2 and 4 are the added ones (parity bits); the other four are your data. Now open the same word with the fifth bit wrong , as if it had changed along the way (in the tool it is the one labeled p5, under Simulate an error ; you can also change it yourself by clicking on it). The tool answers "Corrected - error at position 5" , and nobody told it which one it was. Next: the word with the fifth and second bits wrong . Two bits changed. The answer is “Corrected — error at position 7” , and 7 was fine. The decoder has just changed a correct bit and treats the result as good: the four data bits that come out are no longer 1011 but 1110. (The warning box that appears below is added by the tool to explain it; a real decoder would not show it.) Finally, the same two errors with SECDED turned on (SECDED is a variant explained below). Now the answer is “Double error detected” . What just happened In a computer’s memory, a bit can change by itself because of electrical noise or alpha particles, as Synopsys, which designs memory controllers explains; and a message traveling over a cable or through the air can also arrive with a bit changed. The simplest way to find out is the parity bit : you add a bit that makes the total number of ones always even. If it arrives odd, something has changed. But it only says that there is an error, not where it is. What Richard Hamming did was use several parity bits, each one watching a different group of positions, and make those groups overlap. You have it in the Coverage of each parity bit table of the tool: P1 watches positions 1, 3, 5 and 7. P2 watches positions 2, 3, 6 and 7. P4 watches positions 4, 5, 6 and 7. When bit 5 changes, the two that watch it, P1 and P4, complain, but P2 does not. Add up the ones that complain: 1 + 4 = 5. That sum is the position of the error. The tool writes it as “syndrome 5 = 101₂” : in binary, each digit says whether a check has failed (P4 yes, P2 no, P1 yes). It is called a syndrome, as in medicine: the set of symptoms points to where the problem is. If you want to follow this process step by step, with all the rules and much more detail, it is explained in Hamming Code: Error Detection and Correction . However, with two errors, the self-correcting trick backfires. Bit 5 makes P1 and P4 complain; bit 2, P2. All three complain, 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, and the code, which is built on the assumption that there is only one error, points at position 7 and treats the word as corrected, even though it is still wrong. SECDED ( Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection ) adds one more bit, P0 , which goes in front of all the others and watches the parity of the whole word. That is why with SECDED the word has eight bits instead of seven. With one error, the two clues agree and it is corrected. With two, the groups say that something is wrong but the total parity adds up; that is only possible if an even number of bits has changed, so instead of “correcting” it warns of a double error. The idea was born out of an annoyance. In the late 1940s, Hamming used a relay computer at Bell Labs that, when it detected an error and there were no operators around (at night and on weekends), abandoned the job and moved on to the next one. Weekends were exactly when Hamming worked, and every error forced him to start his programs from scratch. In a taped interview, he said: “Damn it, if the machine can detect an error, why can’t it locate the position of the error and correct it?” ( Hamming code , on Wikipedia , which cites the interview). He published the answer in 1950, in the Bell System Technical Journal . And it is still in use: the DDR4 memory modules with ECC ( error-correcting code ) in servers use a SECDED scheme with 8 check bits for every 64 data bits ( Synopsys ). The classic mistake You might think parity bits are wasted space: in the example, 3 out of every 7 bits carry no data. But that cost drops quickly as the block grows (you can check it in “Try it yourself”, below), and what it buys is the ability to fix an error without asking for the message again. The second confusion is more dangerous: reading “Corrected” as “correct”. The code guarantees what it promises only if what it assumes holds (at most one error per word). Beyond that, it does not stop or warn: it returns a wrong answer with the same confidence as a good one. It is a behavior worth recognizing early, because any system that always gives an answer behaves the same way, AI models included. Try it yourself In the Encode tab of the Hamming Code tool, type any 11 data bits and see how many parity bits the tool adds and what rate (the part of the word that is data) comes out. Before doing it with 26 bits, make a guess: how many parity bits will it need? Check it. Then open the Simulator : send some data 2000 times over a channel where each bit has a 2% chance of getting corrupted. Click Simulate with SECDED off and again with . Look at the Silent failure line. Then raise the probability to 10%. Why does the silent failure grow much faster than the failure probability of each bit? Think about what has to happen for there to be one. The simulator’s numbers are random, so they change a little on each run; what matters is how they move when you change the settings.
